DOCUMENT:
Review of the Graduate Hiring Process: 2025 Intake
Talent Acquisition, Halden Engineering, January 2026

1. Purpose
This review assesses the 2025 graduate recruitment cycle, which opened on 1 September 2024 and closed with final offers on 30 April 2025, and recommends how sourcing budget should be allocated for the 2026 intake. The 2026 hiring target is 100 graduates, against 95 hired in 2025.

2. The process
Candidates complete an online application and numerical reasoning test, followed by a 30-minute phone screen. Those who pass attend a one-day assessment centre with a group exercise and a technical interview, after which offers are made within five working days. Median time from application to offer was 47 days, slightly better than the 52 days recorded for the 2024 intake.

Candidates were sourced through three channels: careers fairs at nine partner universities, paid listings on two graduate job boards, and the employee referral scheme, which pays a £1,000 bonus for each referred graduate who accepts an offer.

3. Funnel by channel
Table 1. 2025 intake by source
Source | Applications | Interviewed | Offers | Accepted | Left within 12 months
University careers fairs | 1,150 | 138 | 46 | 39 | 3
Job boards | 3,400 | 204 | 51 | 34 | 11
Employee referrals | 420 | 84 | 28 | 22 | 2
Total | 4,970 | 426 | 125 | 95 | 16

Overall, 8.6% of applicants reached the assessment centre, 29% of those interviewed received offers and 76% of offers were accepted. Job boards generated by far the largest volume of applications, though a lower proportion of them progressed: 6% of job-board applicants reached interview, compared with 12% from careers fairs and 20% from referrals.

Employee referrals produced the highest offer acceptance rate of any channel, which we attribute to the realistic picture of the company that referrers give their contacts before they apply.

4. Cost by channel
Table 2. Sourcing cost by channel
Source | Channel cost | Hires | Cost per hire
University careers fairs | £58,500 | 39 | £1,500
Job boards | £20,400 | 34 | £600
Employee referrals | £22,000 | 22 | £1,000

Careers-fair costs include stand fees, travel and accommodation for staff, and printed materials. Job-board costs are annual listing fees. Referral costs are bonuses paid.

Across all channels we spent £100,900 for 95 hires, an average of £1,240 per hire, above the sector benchmark of £1,150 per graduate hire reported in the Institute of Student Employers' latest survey. Bringing our cost per hire below the benchmark is therefore a priority for 2026.

5. Candidate experience and onboarding
The post-process candidate survey (312 responses) rated the assessment centre positively, with 84% describing it as fair. The main complaint was the gap between the phone screen and the assessment centre invitation, which averaged 16 days. We will introduce self-scheduling for assessment-centre slots to reduce this.

Graduates spend their first year on a structured rotation programme. Learning and Development estimates the cost of a graduate leaving during the first year, including programme costs, supervisor time and re-recruitment, at around £18,000 per leaver.

6. Recommendations for 2026
6.1 Reduce careers-fair attendance from nine universities to three, retaining only the three that produced the most hires, and cut the fair budget from £58,500 to about £19,500.
6.2 Reallocate the £39,000 saved to additional job-board listings and sponsored placement on a third board. Job boards deliver hires at £600 each, less than half the cost of careers fairs, so shifting volume towards them will allow us to reach the 2026 target of 100 hires while bringing average cost per hire well below the sector benchmark.
6.3 Keep the referral scheme unchanged.
6.4 Introduce self-scheduling for assessment centres and set a target of ten days from phone screen to invitation.

7. Conclusion
The 2025 process worked: we came close to target, candidates rated the assessment fairly and time-to-offer improved. The main weakness is cost efficiency. Rebalancing the sourcing mix towards job boards, our lowest-cost channel, addresses that directly without changing the selection process that candidates and hiring managers value.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [misread_evidence] at: "Employee referrals produced the highest offer acceptance rate of any channel" -- Table 1 gives acceptance rates of 39/46 = 84.8% for careers fairs, 34/51 = 66.7% for job boards and 22/28 = 78.6% for referrals. Careers fairs, not referrals, had the highest acceptance rate.
2. [arithmetic] at: "Across all channels we spent £100,900 for 95 hires, an average of £1,240 per hire" -- £100,900 / 95 = £1,062 per hire, not £1,240. Correctly computed, the company is already below the £1,150 benchmark, undermining the stated priority.
3. [missing_consideration] at: "Job boards deliver hires at £600 each, less than half the cost of careers fairs, so shifting volume towards them will allow us to reach the 2026 target" -- The recommendation compares channels only on sourcing cost per hire, ignoring the first-year attrition in Table 1 (job boards 11/34 = 32% left within 12 months vs 3/39 = 8% for fairs) and the document's own estimate of about £18,000 per first-year leaver. On the document's figures, job-board hires are far more expensive once attrition is counted, and retained headcount toward the target would fall.

REVIEW:
# Review: Graduate Hiring Process, 2025 Intake

**Verdict:** The recommendations don't follow from the evidence. One headline figure is wrong, one claim contradicts the document's own table, and the central recommendation ignores the attrition data in Table 1. The funnel arithmetic otherwise checks out.

## Factual errors

**1. Average cost per hire is miscalculated, and the stated problem doesn't exist (Section 4).**
£100,900 ÷ 95 = **£1,062**, not £1,240. That is *below* the £1,150 benchmark, not above it. The claim that bringing cost below benchmark is "a priority" rests on this error, and so does the framing in 6.2 and the conclusion that "the main weakness is cost efficiency."

**2. Referrals do not have the highest acceptance rate (Section 3).**
From Table 1:
- Careers fairs: 39/46 = **85%**
- Referrals: 22/28 = **79%**
- Job boards: 34/51 = **67%**

Careers fairs are highest. The explanation about referrers giving a realistic picture of the company is therefore unsupported. Referrals do lead on interview rate (20%).

## Flaws in the reasoning

**3. The job-board recommendation ignores attrition, which reverses the conclusion.**
Table 1 shows 11 of 34 job-board hires (**32%**) left within 12 months, against 3 of 39 (8%) for fairs and 2 of 22 (9%) for referrals. At L&D's £18,000 per leaver, the cost per hire including first-year attrition is roughly:

| Channel | Sourcing cost | Leaver cost | Total | Per hire |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Careers fairs | £58,500 | £54,000 | £112,500 | ~£2,885 |
| **Job boards** | £20,400 | **£198,000** | £218,400 | **~£6,425** |
| Referrals | £22,000 | £36,000 | £58,000 | ~£2,640 |

Job boards are the *most* expensive channel once leavers are counted, and referrals are the cheapest. Total leaver cost (£288,000) is nearly three times the whole sourcing budget, so attrition is the real cost problem. The report never mentions it alongside the £18,000 figure.

**4. £600 is an average cost, not a marginal one.**
Job-board costs are annual listing fees. Adding listings and a third board won't necessarily yield hires at £600 each, and a 6% interview rate suggests diminishing returns as volume grows. The recommendation assumes linear scaling without evidence.

**5. The cut to careers fairs isn't tied to expected hires.**
Cutting from nine fairs to three and from £58,500 to £19,500 assumes equal cost per fair. The retained three produce more than a third of the hires, but the report doesn't say how many (it should). Fair hires will drop by some number, and the report doesn't estimate how many job-board hires are needed to replace them, or whether the target of 100 is reachable. Replacement hires from boards would also carry the higher attrition rate.

**6. Referrals are underused.**
Referrals have the best interview rate (20%), near-best attrition (9%) and the lowest all-in cost per hire. "Keep unchanged" is a missed opportunity. Raising the bonus or promoting the scheme deserves consideration.

## Smaller points

- "Came close to target" can't be assessed because the 2025 target isn't stated.
- The survey had 312 responses, and the report doesn't give a response rate or say who was surveyed. An 84% "fair" rating could reflect selection bias, since offered candidates may respond more often.
- The 16-day gap between phone screen and invitation is a good finding. The 10-day target is reasonable, but the report doesn't say whether it affects drop-out.
- The report doesn't explain why job-board hires leave at such a high rate (role mismatch, weaker screening, less realistic expectations?). Fix the cause before scaling the channel.

## Suggested revisions

- Correct the average cost per hire to £1,062 and drop the "above benchmark" framing.
- Correct the acceptance-rate claim and remove or rework the referral explanation.
- Add attrition-adjusted cost per hire by channel and rebuild the budget recommendation on it.
- Reconsider 6.2. Likely directions are a modest fair reduction, more investment in referrals, and an investigation of job-board attrition before any expansion.
- Show a hires forecast by channel for 2026 demonstrating how 100 hires would be reached.
